title: New Housing Fund Rules: Take What You Can, but Don't Treat It as Savings
dek: The housing provident fund is not savings you can withdraw at will; fraudulent withdrawal gets you pursued and barred from any withdrawal for three years. But the new rules put renting first in the withdrawal order and scrap the rent-to-income ratio cap — money you should take, you should still take.
why: Three people in different situations — a self-employed worker, a young professional, a property owner — each run their own numbers, turning the 20 clause changes in the new rules into concrete decisions. The second half on flexible-employment contributions and the comparison with the system-inside track is especially informative.
who: Employees with a provident fund who aren't sure whether to withdraw or leave it; people considering buying a home, converting a commercial loan to a provident fund loan, or contributing as flexible-employment workers; job seekers trying to judge whether a company is well-run.
skip: The opening chit-chat about the show's origin and the three hosts' positions can be fast-forwarded; start from 13:10, when Zhou Yi's experience of using it.

points.h: Six months after auto-withdrawal, I paused it myself
points.body: After Zhou Yi activated Beijing's no-threshold monthly rent withdrawal of 2,000 yuan, she found the money slid into another card the moment it arrived, completely decoupled from the mental account for paying rent. By month's end, once her spending card was maxed out, it was automatically deducted from that card, adding friction to daily life. After confirming the fund balance earns 1.5% interest — higher than the roughly 0.95% on a one-year bank time deposit — she paused the withdrawal the next day. Yu Bai noted this contrasts with the advice three years ago to ‘take everything you're entitled to and use everything you can’; two young colleagues in the department had made the same choice. Lao Qian cautioned that this is indeed inefficient use of funds, but most people can't achieve the efficiency they imagine — people just cook their own books.

points.h: The housing fund is not savings; not being able to withdraw is the norm
points.body: Yu Bai walked through an extreme scenario: a young person loses their job and goes home with no liquid funds, a few tens of thousands in the provident fund, but the home is owner-occupied, so it qualifies neither as a home purchase nor as renting. Even if the new rules allow withdrawal for renovation or property fees, if the family has no such needs, there's nothing to be done. If you risk fraudulent withdrawal under a fabricated pretext, you'll be pursued to return the full amount and barred from any withdrawal for three years. So both approaches hold — ‘take everything you're entitled to’ and ‘treat it as forced savings at a higher rate than a demand deposit’ — the key is the individual situation.

points.h: The new rules put renting first in the withdrawal order
points.body: This revision adjusts 20 clauses in total. First, renovating an owner-occupied home and paying property fees for an owner-occupied home are included in the withdrawal scope for the first time; the fund no longer serves only loan-based home purchases. Second, renting withdrawal previously required rent to exceed a set proportion of household wage income; this version removes that restriction, and renting is placed first in the withdrawal order. Third, flexible-employment workers are formally brought into the system for the first time — self-employed individuals and part-time workers can contribute voluntarily and apply for provident fund loans. In addition, the management center must reply to withdrawal applications within three days and to loan applications within ten days, and nationwide mutual recognition of contribution records is being advanced.

points.h: The share of contributions lent out has fallen from 70% to 30%
points.body: The figure Lao Qian saw: this year, the share of provident fund contributions lent out is as low as just over 30%, while at the peak it was over 70% — a steady decline in just a few years. In other words, the theoretically most stable, lowest-rate, highest-quality lending channel is actually used by only just over 30% of people. This directly reflects how low the willingness to buy homes is. Lao Qian also points out the new rules point toward housing consumption rather than leverage: renting moved to first place, property fees and renovation can be withdrawn, thresholds greatly lowered — supporting measures as the real estate market shifts from an incremental to a stock phase, and also echoing aging: the monthly withdrawal ratio turned up in 2023, exactly corresponding to the 1960s cohort retiring.

points.h: If you want to buy a home, be careful about withdrawing
points.body: Yu Bai warns: the provident fund loan amount is tied to the account balance — in some cities you can borrow 16 times the balance, in others 20 times, varying by city. Guangzhou also has multiple caps; when applying, the smallest of several standards applies. For example, for a first or second owner-occupied home the minimum down payment is 20%, so a 1 million yuan home can't be loaned more than 800,000; and monthly repayment exceeding 50% of monthly income is also disallowed. So before withdrawing the fund as living expenses, check your city's loan rules. Yu Bai is also cautious about the buy logic of ‘rent-to-price ratio close to the provident fund rate, only a down payment short’: you also have to consider depreciation, price fluctuations, and how to withstand risk once a 600,000 down payment is locked up.

points.h: Flexible-employment contributors carry the full amount alone
points.body: For flexible-employment workers, the contribution base and rate are calculated the same as for employees, but there's no employer paying half — effectively one person bears the full 10% to 24%. The contribution base must be self-declared: below 10,000 no proof is needed; above 10,000 you must log into the individual income tax app and check your tax details as documentation, to prevent over-declaring to extract a higher loan amount. Zhou Yi did the math: 10,000 at 10% to 24% is 1,000 to 2,400 yuan, and this money isn't counted in income tax, but if you don't use it you lose out. In addition, most pilot cities require 6 to 12 consecutive months of contributions before applying for a provident fund loan, and most don't allow retroactive lump-sum payments.

points.h: Inside the system, the provident fund is an invisible benefit
points.body: Zhou Yi asked a friend with a public institution post back home, who openly showed a screenshot of her provident fund account: monthly deposits were more than double Zhou Yi's, and the balance already exceeded her savings. The friend lives at home with no rental need, so the fund just accumulates as forced savings or future loan capacity, plus an occupational annuity, with the contribution base including all bonuses and subsidies. Lao Qian adds: the provident fund is tax-free, and with the individual pension capped at 12,000 yuan a year and taxed at 3% on withdrawal, those inside the system already get an extra layer of tax advantage. On the data: in 2025 the national average annual wage for urban non-private unit employees was 129,441 yuan, for private units 71,590 yuan — while working hours run the other way.

points.h: Full provident fund contributions are a slice for judging a company
points.body: Lao Qian's judgment on ‘is a company that pays the provident fund a better choice’ hasn't changed at all: a company that pays the full provident fund shows it respects employees and respects the rules, meaning it's likely well-run in every aspect, not playing games with policy. He goes further: this points to not making profit maximization the first goal, treating people as people, and the invisible returns show up elsewhere. Zhou Yi did the math: a wage base of 100, take-home just over 70, but the boss pays over 130 — everyone in the chain feels aggrieved. Lao Qian cites Ford's Model T wage increase — letting workers afford a car and have time to use it wasn't capitalist conscience, it was a better utility function.

quotes.text: It arrived, but because your phone app has so many notifications, you don't look carefully — say it reminds you 2,000 yuan came in, and it just sits in that card until the end of the month, when my spending card is maxed out and it gets automatically deducted from that card.
But the fact is people cook their own books, people withdraw on impulse for all sorts of reasons, people are very good at self-deception.
You really can't treat the provident fund as savings, because your bank savings you can withdraw at any time, but the provident fund you can't.
And it's the highest-quality lending channel, the rate is so low, yet only just over 30% of people took loans — at the peak, what was that share? Over 70% — in just a few years.
I think a company that pays the full provident fund shows it respects employees and respects the rules.

Treating people as people doesn't mean increasing costs — it also means one person's spending, household sector spending, becomes corporate sector income, and corporate sector spending becomes household sector wages; the two form a virtuous cycle.
Take everything you're entitled to and use everything you can — buying a home, building, renovating, repaying a loan, renting, retirement, leaving the country — all can use it.
